::: {#exm-early-stopping}

#### Stopping at the lowest validation loss

```{python}
#| code-fold: show
stopped_net = make_net()
_ = stopped_net.load_state_dict(plain_best_state)
with torch.no_grad():
    test_loss_stopped = loss_fn(stopped_net(x_test), y_test).item()
    test_loss_final = loss_fn(plain_net(x_test), y_test).item()
acc_stopped = accuracy(stopped_net, x_test, y_test)
acc_final = accuracy(plain_net, x_test, y_test)
print(test_loss_stopped, test_loss_final, acc_stopped, acc_final)
```

`fit()` already does [early stopping](#def-early-stopping):
it keeps the [parameters](https://morrison-lab.github.io/lds/chapters/big-ideas.html#def-parameter) of [epoch](https://morrison-lab.github.io/lds/chapters/gradient-descent.html#def-epoch) `r py$best_epoch` of @sol-overfit-curves.
On the `r py$n_test` test images,
those parameters have loss `r sprintf("%.3f", py$test_loss_stopped)`,
against `r sprintf("%.3f", py$test_loss_final)` after all 300 [epochs](https://morrison-lab.github.io/lds/chapters/gradient-descent.html#def-epoch).
The test accuracies are `r sprintf("%.1f", 100 * py$acc_stopped)`% and `r sprintf("%.1f", 100 * py$acc_final)`%.
The [accuracy](https://morrison-lab.github.io/lds/chapters/metrics.html#def-accuracy) moves much less than the loss,
because the loss also measures how much probability the network gives the true digit,
not only whether that digit gets the most.

:::
